newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt leaves dlr bloc in dust after welcome data.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt leaves dlr bloc in dust after welcome data.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close

* NZ debt rallies across curve post-CPI
* Good qtrly out-turn reinforces scope for easier conditions
* U.S. inflation data could temper bonds' rally
New Zealand debt put in a sterling performance on Tuesday in the wake of surprisingly soft March quarter inflation data.
The 90-day bank bill rate ended 19 basis points lower at 7.38 percent, while its futures counterpart was 22 points stronger at 92.47 on very solid volume of 6,820 contracts.
The currency's Trade-Weighted Index closed around 68.60, from its 68.68 finish on Monday.
The market was pleasantly surprised by data from Statistics New Zealand showing headline inflation down 0.3 percent in the March quarter for a 1.8 percent annual rise.
Market economists polled before the data had on average forecast a 0.11 percent quarterly rise in the CPI and 2.19 percent for the year.
Shortly after the CPI release, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand calculated underlying inflation was 0.22 percent in the quarter for an annual rate of 1.97 percent.
The bank had expected 0.5 percent quarterly core inflation (2.2 percent annual), and market expectations were a fraction below that.

"One had the strong feeling that the market going into this announcement was positioned long (in) interest rate products, long (in) bank bills and futures, and short (in) the TWI as a hedging mechanism," a Wellington dealer said.
"That could explain why the currency hasn't gone down a lot."
The dealer saw scope for short rates to fall another 20 basis points, especially as the TWI was holding in well.
Dealers said monetary conditions were still tighter than the RBNZ's ideal but had come within the bank's tolerance band, reducing the chance of a central bank comment.
Bonds ended 10 to 15 basis points stronger, after a good start on the back of overnight offshore buying in the 02/01 maturity and a NZ$100 million 05/02 Eurokiwi issued by a Commerzbank unit.

Dealers said while bonds had gained on the back of the inflation data they remained susceptible to global movements, and could retrace if U.S. Treasuries sold off on the back of that country's CPI data due at 1230 GMT.
